routes.description: Establish that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent personal ground, identify God's nature and authority as that ground, and show why evolutionary or material descriptions cannot supply binding normativity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects moral objectivity, obligation, and purpose to an invariant personal source while answering the principal naturalistic, arbitrariness, and moral-knowledge alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that God, understood as the personal ground of goodness and obligation, explains objective morality more completely than science, evolution, and human flourishing alone.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective moral comparison, binding duties, and human purpose require a standard, authority, and telos beyond individual or social opinion.
Explain why empirical and evolutionary accounts of behavior do not by themselves generate prescriptive duties or an objective hierarchy among competing moral dispositions.
Defend God's nature as the nonarbitrary moral standard rather than locating goodness outside God or in contingent commands.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect trustworthy reasoning, freedom, and moral agency to a conception of persons not exhausted by blind material processes.
Distinguish questions about knowing or interpreting moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objective.

routes.description: Establish an objective moral framework centered on sentient interests, autonomy, liberty, and flourishing; explain its evolutionary and empirical basis; and challenge the necessity and reliability of divine grounding.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if evolved moral capacities and reasoned attention to individual welfare support objective moral judgment while divine-command, scriptural, and theistic accounts face unresolved explanatory or epistemic objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that science, evolution, and principles of sentient flourishing can explain objective moral capacities and judgments without requiring a supernatural personal ground.

centralBridges.description: Account for empathy, fairness, reciprocity, and cooperation as evolved capacities that make moral understanding and social life possible.
Specify survival, flourishing, autonomy, liberty, and equal consideration as standards for judging conduct and constraining aggregate welfare.
Show why rival revelations, interpretive disagreement, historical revision, or contingent commands impede a reliable divine or scriptural moral method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain moral progress through widening equal consideration, reform led by affected persons, and correction through evidence and reason.
Test whether suffering and the history of religious moral practice cohere with a perfectly good divine moral ground.

sections.title: The Ground of Objective Standards and Duties
sections.rationale: This section addresses the motion's primary ontological burden: whether objective moral standards and binding obligations require a personal divine source or can exist within a naturalistic account.

sections.title: Evolution, Flourishing, and the Is–Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: This section tests whether evolved capacities, cooperation, sentient welfare, autonomy, and flourishing can support prescriptive moral judgments rather than merely describe behavior and survival.

sections.title: Divine Authority, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: This section covers the relationship between moral grounding and moral access, including divine-command arbitrariness, scriptural interpretation, religious diversity, and the distinction between ontology and epistemology.

sections.title: Reason, Agency, and the Nature of Persons
sections.rationale: This section examines whether material and evolutionary processes can sustain trustworthy reasoning and responsible moral agency, or whether those capacities require an immaterial or theistic basis.

sections.title: Moral Progress, Rights, and Difficult Applications
sections.rationale: This section tests each framework through historical reform and contested cases involving equal rights, liberty, suffering, and conflicts between individual autonomy and collective welfare.

components.text: Whether the transplant dilemma demonstrates objective individual value and a principled constraint on welfare.
Whether an evolutionary worldview can recognize human value and morally significant dilemmas.

response.rationale: The reply directly interprets the dilemma as evidence of objective value, but its move from value to a divine lawgiver and its naturalist caricature remain unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: Evolutionary worldview is treated as implying that humans are valueless germs, conflating natural origin with nihilism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that naturalism makes every choice morally indifferent is radically stronger than the supplied argument.

charity.alternative: A naturalistic account can assign moral status through sentience, interests, autonomy, or flourishing despite evolutionary origins.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling humans overgrown germs does not address those proposed value-conferring properties.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Evolution and material processes describe what survives but cannot prescribe what ought to survive or impose binding duties to cooperate rather than exploit.

sourceSpan.excerpt: evolution describes what does survive not what ought to survive why humans and which humans why not the Nazis rather than us should we rape to survive I mean if it's all about survival you can survive and get your genes in another person by raping them should you do that also should we murder the weak to help others to survive Michael and to his credit said no but that's exactly what Hitler did using natural selection

moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted closing statement uses Turek's characteristic first-person references to Michael and develops the pro side's naturalism critique.

components.text: Whether survival and flourishing can generate prescriptions about what and whose interests ought to be protected.
Whether evolved cooperative capacities establish duties rather than describe dispositions.
Whether autonomy supplies a non-survival normative constraint.

response.rationale: The response squarely presses the is-ought and selection problems against survival and evolved cooperation, but it does not address the later autonomy constraint.

precisionFindings.rationale: Materialism is reduced to chemistry and biology, and the con framework is narrowed to survival despite its explicit flourishing and rights elements.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The is-ought criticism is strong, but the categorical dismissal understates the con side's additional normative premises.

charity.alternative: The con framework proposes flourishing, sentient interests, rights, and autonomy in addition to evolutionary descriptions of survival.
charity.decisiveQualification: The is-ought demand remains live, but answering only survival does not exhaust that framework.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The descriptive-prescriptive objection and question of whose survival are coherent, but the reduction of the rival view to survival is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual category distinction is relevant, though the examples do not compare the con side's full normative bridge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks completion of the con naturalistic-ground motion bridge.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive naturalistic prescription component while leaving one important rights-based qualification unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes what survives from what ought to survive and asks why cooperation or human survival should prevail over exploitation.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Minds, logical laws, moral values, love, and justice are immaterial realities that cannot be reduced to matter, so persons are more than physical machines.

sourceSpan.excerpt: minds laws of logic laws of mathematics laws of nature the very laws that you need to do science are immaterial I mean the law of gravity is immaterial we can see its effect but it's not a physical thing it affects physical things but it's not a physical thing itself the laws of morality love and justice these are immaterial things that can't be explained by molecules in motion

moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted closing statement remains in Turek's voice and explicitly opposes Michael's materialism while advancing a soul-body distinction.

components.text: Whether science and reason provide practical methods for correcting harmful moral beliefs.
Whether evolved physical organisms can instantiate moral cognition and fairness.

response.rationale: The immateriality claim bears on physical realization of moral cognition but does not answer whether scientific reasoning functions as a corrective method.

precisionFindings.rationale: Mind, abstract laws, regularities, values, love, and justice are grouped as immaterial things despite important category differences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Nonphysical description or abstract status does not by itself show that molecular systems cannot explain cognition or instantiate values.

charity.alternative: A naturalist can distinguish abstract propositions and laws from physically realized minds and socially instantiated evaluative relations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling each item immaterial does not show that none can be realized, known, or explained through physical systems.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion that persons exceed matter does not follow from grouping abstract laws, values, and mental phenomena as immaterial.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples demonstrate that concepts and laws are not ordinary physical objects, but not the claimed explanatory impossibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro reason-and-agency bridge through an asserted irreducibility of mind.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (54 and 52); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts a secondary physical-realization issue while leaving the primary methodological demand unaddressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt groups minds, logic, mathematics, natural laws, morality, love, and justice as immaterial and declares them inexplicable by molecules.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Goodness is neither external to God nor arbitrarily invented by divine command because God's unchanging nature is itself the objective moral standard.

components.text: Whether divine morality is arbitrary or dependent on an external standard rather than grounded in God's nature.

components.text: Whether matter and evolutionary history can produce beings capable of genuine moral knowledge and wisdom.
